agent.installLead: One command, and one key. Everything below is optional.
agent.lead: An agent that lives in your terminal and does the work — not a chat window that describes it.
agent.modelsBody: One OpenRouter key reaches a hundred models. Native keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and DeepSeek work directly, several keys per provider rotate on rate limits, and a local model through Ollama needs no key at all. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works by pointing one setting at it.
agent.title: Chimera Agent
agent.what1: Solves a task end to end
agent.what1Body: It plans, edits files, runs the verification command, and reverts the whole attempt if the check fails. A run that changed nothing on disk is reported as a failure, not a success — and every receipt names which authority approved it: a test, a diff, a reviewing model, or nothing.
agent.what2Body: Several tasks run at once, each in its own git worktree, so parallel agents cannot edit the same file behind each other's backs. Safe edits are merged; conflicts are reported rather than guessed at.
agent.what3Body: Short-term, recent, factual and about-you memory with a relation graph and a full-text store, plus natural-language scheduling so it runs without being asked.
agent.what4Body: Files, a shell, a real rendered browser, any MCP server, web search, image generation, speech, media download, data analysis and charts. Messaging on Discord, Telegram, Slack, Signal and WhatsApp, plus an HTTP endpoint.

caveat.alphaNotGa: Internal surface coverage — how much of the codebase is proven by real tests. It is not a statement about the product, which is alpha.
caveat.easySlice: A deliberately easy, single-repo slice of SWE-bench Verified. This is not a SWE-bench Verified score — a real one needs the full 500 instances. The delta is not significant on its own.
caveat.internalSuite: Measured on our own Docker-free suite, graded by pytest — one model, small self-contained Python tasks. This is not SWE-bench, and it does not generalise to real repositories.
caveat.publishedNegative: The scaffold did not help here, and the run is published as measured. Both arms sit near the floor and the difference is not significant.
caveat.retracted: Retracted. Seven pre-registered runs; the one positive result did not survive a higher-powered replication, so the claim was withdrawn rather than kept.

coverage.body: Tier 1 is everything a visitor reads before deciding whether to stay — navigation, the home page, the product pages, downloads, and every caveat. It is complete in every language, and CI refuses a build where it is not. Tier 2 is the reference material: the command list, the evidence page furniture, the blog and the skills hub. Those fall back to English behind a notice that says so.
coverage.ratchet: The English column is the key set. A machine-translated technical reference that has drifted out of date is not accessibility — it is a confident lie with an accent, and it is why the second tier is allowed to wait.

desktop.installBody: Native installers for Windows, macOS and Linux. No Python needed — the backend is bundled.
desktop.lead: The app you work in: conversation that edits code, a board that dispatches to your agents, and the settings that actually apply.
desktop.screen1Body: A conversation that edits your repository, with the real history of what it did — every tool call, every file touched, and the option to revert.
desktop.screen2Body: Runs and receipts: what each attempt cost, what approved it, and whether the configuration was worth it, project by project.
desktop.screen3Body: Memory and skills — what the agent has kept, what it learned, and what is waiting for your review before it is used.
desktop.screen4Body: Schedules, a task board with a lane per agent, and projects that run against a spec until the spec says they are done.
desktop.screen5Body: Models, memory, autonomy, tools and your agent's own name, language and standing instructions. Each one says when it takes effect.

download.alphaBody: Solid and heavily tested, without production mileage. Start with low-stakes work, and keep the sandbox in mind for anything that touches real systems.
download.appBody: No Python needed — the backend is bundled with the app.
download.requirementsBody: Windows x86_64, macOS on Apple silicon and Intel, and Linux x86_64 with webkit2gtk-4.1. The project does not declare a minimum operating system version, so this page does not invent one — if an install fails on yours, that is worth reporting.
download.signedBody: The app updates itself from a Minisign-signed manifest, so an update cannot be swapped for something else in transit. That is a separate mechanism from the installer warning above, and it is worth knowing about.
download.signedHeading: Updates are signed, even though the installer is not
download.subtitle: Native installers for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus the terminal agent from PyPI.
download.terminalBody: Python 3.11 to 3.13. The lean install is the first line; the second brings everything that is not GPU-bound.
download.title: Download
download.unsignedBody: There is no code-signing certificate, so the first run is blocked by the operating system. This is expected, and it is the only warning you should have to click through.
download.unsignedLinux: Linux: make the AppImage executable with chmod +x before running it.
download.unsignedMacos: macOS: Gatekeeper refuses a double-click. Right-click the app and choose Open, then confirm.
download.unsignedWindows: Windows: SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC". Choose More info, then Run anyway.

home.agentBlurb: The harness: a right hand in your terminal. It plans, edits, runs the check, and reverts itself when the check fails.
home.alphaBody: Solid and heavily tested, not yet battle-hardened in production. The installers are not signed by a certificate authority, so Windows and macOS warn on first run. Both of those are on the download page too, before the button.
home.alphaHeading: It is alpha, and it says so
home.desktopBlurb: The app: conversation that edits code, a board that dispatches to your agents, and every setting the agent has — on Windows, macOS and Linux.
home.evidenceCta: See every number, with its caveats
home.lead: A terminal agent that does real work on its own, and a desktop app to work with it. Open source, runs on your machine, and publishes the benchmarks where it lost.
home.panelBody: The lion, the goat, the dragon and the snake were on the logo before they were an argument. A panel of models answers, a judge names where they agree and where they do not, and a synthesiser writes the result — but only when the question is hard enough to be worth it. Fusion itself is not unique; wiring it into the agent loop behind a cost-aware router, and measuring it, is.
home.pillar1Body: Other agents learn by appending what happened. Chimera keeps a learned change only when a verified result proves it helped — gated on the real working-tree diff and an honest A/B, never on what the model says about itself. Whether that accumulation makes it better at new tasks is measured, and the answer so far is on the evidence page.
home.pillar2Body: Prompt injection is widely considered unpatchable, and most agents mitigate it in the application layer or declare it out of scope. There is a real defence layer here — taint tracking, control tokens stripped from untrusted content, dangerous tools narrowed for the rest of a tainted run, side-effecting retries protected — and it is opt-in and off by default, which the security page states before it states anything else.
home.pillar3Body: Every figure comes with a confidence interval, the runs that went nowhere are published unchanged, and a claim that stops surviving replication is withdrawn. Nothing on this site is typed by hand; it is read from the snapshot the product stamps at each release.
home.pillarsHeading: Three bets, and where each one stands

press.clearance: Give the mark clear space of at least a quarter of its width on every side, do not recolour it, and do not place it on a busy photograph.
press.coloursBody: The site and the desktop app read the same tokens from the same file, so these are the product's colours, not an interpretation of them.
press.fileIcon: The mark on its navy plate — the app icon, and the safe choice at any size.
press.fileMark: The mark with the plate removed. Correct on a dark ground only: taking the navy out also took the dark facet lines inside the mane, which were the same colour. On a light background it looks moth-eaten, which is why the site always puts it on a disc.
press.fileWide: The horizontal lockup, mark and wordmark.
press.markBody: A lion, a goat, a dragon and a cobra, low-poly and lit cyan. It exists only as raster — there is no vector source, and the wordmark you see in headings is set in type rather than scaled from the logo file, because a 2241-pixel image is soft on any modern display above about 700 CSS pixels.
press.markGap: A vector of the mark is a real gap, tracked rather than hidden. Until it exists, use the PNGs below at or under their natural size, and never scale the wordmark image.
press.subtitle: The mark, the colours, and what this project can and cannot grant you.
press.title: Brand
press.usageBody: The code is Apache-2.0, and that licence grants no trademark rights — section 6 says so explicitly. In practice: writing about Chimera, linking to it, and showing the mark to refer to the project are all fine. Putting the mark on something that is not this project, or on a product that suggests endorsement, is not, and there is no trademark policy to point you at yet.
privacy.body: This site sets no cookies, runs no analytics, and asks for nothing. It is a folder of static files served from a server in Europe; that server keeps ordinary access logs, which contain IP addresses and are not used for anything but keeping the site up. There is no account, no newsletter, and no third-party script — the pages load nothing from a domain that is not this one.
privacy.contact: Questions go to the issue tracker.
privacy.downloads: Downloading the app takes you to GitHub, and downloading the terminal agent takes you to PyPI. Both are separate services with their own policies.

skills.installBody: The card is data. Clone the repository and import it by path — anything that arrives over the network is treated as tainted and held for approval, which is the behaviour you want and the reason there is no one-line installer here.
skills.integrityBody: SHA-256 of the file as published. An importer can check that what it received is what this page showed.
skills.positioning: Fewer cards, each with a name behind it. Every card here was reviewed by a maintainer before it merged, carries the provenance that review conferred, and is served with a hash of the exact bytes on this page. That is the part a catalogue of ninety thousand entries cannot offer.
skills.provenanceCleanBody: Conferred by a reviewer who read the card, not claimed by the file about itself. A card the agent distils during a run that consumed untrusted content is born tainted and is held for review before it is ever retrieved.
skills.subtitle: Short cards that tell the agent how to approach a recurring kind of task. Data, never code — nothing here is executed.
